title: January: Orion at his best
intro: January evenings belong to [[con:Ori|Orion]]. Face south-southeast and look halfway up the sky for three evenly spaced stars in a short straight row: [[asterism:orions-belt|Orion's Belt]]. Orange [[star:Betelgeuse|Betelgeuse]] marks a shoulder above it and blue-white [[star:Rigel|Rigel]] a foot below. This is the brightest region of the whole sky, and all of it survives city lights.

Use the Belt as a pointer. Follow it up and to the right to orange [[star:Aldebaran|Aldebaran]] and the V of [[con:Tau|Taurus]], and on to the little cluster of [[dso:M45|the Pleiades]]. Follow it down and to the left to [[star:Sirius|Sirius]], the brightest star of the night, still low in the southeast. Nearly overhead shines yellow [[star:Capella|Capella]] in [[con:Aur|Auriga]], and to the east the twin stars [[star:Castor|Castor]] and [[star:Pollux|Pollux]] stand one above the other.
Turn around to the north and the W of [[con:Cas|Cassiopeia]] is high in the northwest, with [[con:Per|Perseus]] between it and Capella, while the Big Dipper stands on its handle low in the northeast.

objects.note: The Orion Nebula, the misty middle of Orion's Sword: a cloud where stars are forming.
The Pleiades, a tiny dipper of blue-white stars; glorious in binoculars.
The Hyades, the V-shaped face of the Bull and the nearest open cluster.
A rich open cluster at the foot of Gemini; a dim round patch in binoculars from a dark site.
The Double Cluster between Perseus and Cassiopeia, two knots of stars side by side.

southernNote: From the southern hemisphere Orion stands high in the north and upside down, with Sirius nearly overhead and Canopus high in the south.

title: February: the Winter Hexagon
intro: In February the brilliant winter stars stand due south as darkness falls. Start at [[con:Ori|Orion]] and trace the [[asterism:winter-hexagon|Winter Hexagon]] around him: from [[star:Rigel|Rigel]] down to [[star:Sirius|Sirius]], up to [[star:Procyon|Procyon]], on to [[star:Pollux|Pollux]] and [[star:Castor|Castor]], over the top through [[star:Capella|Capella]] almost overhead, and back down past [[star:Aldebaran|Aldebaran]]. Orange Betelgeuse sits inside the ring.

Sirius is now at its highest, sparkling with flashes of color because we see it through so much air. It leads [[con:CMa|Canis Major]], the big dog at Orion's heel; [[con:Lep|Lepus]] the hare crouches under Orion's feet, and the faint unicorn [[con:Mon|Monoceros]] fills the space between Sirius and Procyon, where the dim winter Milky Way runs.
In the east, the Sickle of Leo is rising, a first hint of spring, and the Big Dipper is climbing in the northeast.

objects.note: The Orion Nebula is still perfectly placed in the early evening.
An open cluster four degrees straight below Sirius, about the width of the full Moon.
Open cluster beside the feet of Gemini, now very high.
The richest of the three Messier clusters in Auriga, a fine dusting of faint stars.
The Beehive cluster in Cancer, climbing in the east between Pollux and Regulus.

southernNote: Southern observers have Sirius and Canopus high overhead and the Southern Cross rising in the southeast in the evening.

title: March: winter west, spring east
intro: March is a month of handover. The [[asterism:winter-hexagon|Winter Hexagon]] still blazes, but it has shifted into the southwest, and Orion is leaning over toward the western horizon. Catch him early in the evening.

High in the south are the twins [[star:Castor|Castor]] and [[star:Pollux|Pollux]] of [[con:Gem|Gemini]], with [[star:Procyon|Procyon]] below them. East of the twins is a dark gap, the faint constellation [[con:Cnc|Cancer]], and then [[con:Leo|Leo]]: look for a backward question mark of stars, [[asterism:sickle-of-leo|the Sickle]], with bright [[star:Regulus|Regulus]] at its base. The Sickle is the lion's head and mane.

In the northeast the [[asterism:big-dipper|Big Dipper]] is standing high on its handle. The faint stars of [[con:Lyn|Lynx]] and [[con:LMi|Leo Minor]] fill the space between the Dipper and the twins, a region that really needs a dark sky.

objects.note: The Beehive, a swarm of stars in the middle of Cancer, is at its highest.
An old, compact open cluster in southern Cancer.
Open cluster at the feet of Gemini, still high in the west.
Bright spiral galaxy above the Dipper's bowl, with M82 beside it; needs a dark sky.
A close double star: a telescope at 100× splits it into two white stars.

southernNote: From the south, Leo appears upside down in the northeast while Canopus, the Southern Cross and the rich Milky Way of Carina ride high.

title: April: the Lion and the Great Bear
intro: On April evenings the [[asterism:big-dipper|Big Dipper]] is almost overhead, upside down, as if pouring out its bowl. It is the key to the spring sky. The two stars at the end of the bowl point north to [[star:Polaris|Polaris]]; go the other way, as if the bowl leaked, and the drips fall on the back of [[con:Leo|Leo]].

Leo stands high in the south: [[asterism:sickle-of-leo|the Sickle]] with [[star:Regulus|Regulus]] in front, and a triangle of stars ending in [[star:Denebola|Denebola]] for the hindquarters and tail. Follow the curve of the Dipper's handle outward to find orange [[star:Arcturus|Arcturus]] rising in the east.

Below Leo sprawls [[con:Hya|Hydra]], the longest constellation; its lone bright star, [[star:Alphard|Alphard]], sits in an empty stretch of the south. Between Leo's tail and Arcturus, away from the Milky Way, lies the realm of galaxies in [[con:Com|Coma Berenices]] and [[con:CVn|Canes Venatici]]. In the west, the last winter stars are setting.

objects.note: The middle star of the Dipper's handle has a faint companion, Alcor; a small telescope splits Mizar itself in two.
Spiral galaxy near the Dipper's bowl, with the streak of M82 in the same view.
The Whirlpool Galaxy near the end of the Dipper's handle; a dark sky is essential.
The Coma Star Cluster, a wide scatter of faint stars that is the 'hair' of Coma Berenices.
The Beehive in Cancer, now in the southwest.

southernNote: Southern observers see Leo low in the north, with the Southern Cross and the Pointers, Alpha and Beta Centauri, climbing high in the southeast.

title: May: follow the arc
intro: May's sky is drawn with one sweeping line. Find the Big Dipper high in the north, follow the curve of its handle away from the bowl, and "arc to Arcturus": [[star:Arcturus|Arcturus]], a brilliant orange star high in the southeast. Keep going the same distance and "speed on to Spica", the blue-white star of [[con:Vir|Virgo]], lower in the south. That is the [[asterism:spring-arc|Spring Arc]].

Arcturus is the base of [[con:Boo|Boötes]], a kite shape stretching up toward the Dipper's handle. Just east of the kite is a neat half-circle of stars, [[con:CrB|Corona Borealis]], the Northern Crown. To the right of Spica, four stars make the lopsided box of [[con:Crv|Corvus]] the crow.

[[con:Leo|Leo]] is now heading down the western sky. Between Leo's tail and Arcturus you are looking straight out of our galaxy, toward thousands of others in [[con:Com|Coma Berenices]] and Virgo. In the northeast, [[star:Vega|Vega]] is rising: summer is on the way.

objects.note: A globular cluster between Arcturus and Cor Caroli; a fuzzy star in binoculars.
The Coma Star Cluster, a loose spray of stars best in binoculars.
The Whirlpool Galaxy near Alkaid, almost overhead on May evenings.
The Sombrero Galaxy on the Virgo–Corvus border, a small spindle of light.
Giant elliptical galaxy at the heart of the Virgo Cluster; needs a dark sky.
An easy, pretty double star under the Dipper's handle.

southernNote: From the south, Arcturus and Spica shine in the north while the Southern Cross stands upright at its highest, with Omega Centauri nearby.

title: June: the Herdsman and the Crown
intro: June nights are short, and it is not fully dark until late. When the stars do come out, the [[asterism:spring-arc|Spring Arc]] is at its best: from the Dipper's handle, now high in the northwest, arc to [[star:Arcturus|Arcturus]] very high in the south and speed on to [[star:Spica|Spica]] in the southwest.

East of the kite of [[con:Boo|Boötes]] comes the little half-ring of [[con:CrB|Corona Borealis]], and east of that the four-star [[asterism:keystone|Keystone]] of [[con:Her|Hercules]], climbing toward the zenith. Under the Crown, the head of the serpent [[con:Ser|Serpens]] is a small triangle of stars. Low in the south, two modest stars mark the scales of [[con:Lib|Libra]], and to their left red [[star:Antares|Antares]] is rising with the claws of Scorpius.

In the north, the Little Dipper stands straight up from [[star:Polaris|Polaris]], and the long body of [[con:Dra|Draco]] winds between the two Dippers. In the east, [[star:Vega|Vega]], [[star:Deneb|Deneb]] and [[star:Altair|Altair]] are all up: the Summer Triangle has arrived.

objects.note: The great globular cluster on the side of the Keystone; a round fuzzy spot in binoculars.
A fine globular cluster in the head of Serpens.
Globular cluster between Arcturus and Cor Caroli, now high in the west.
The brighter scale of Libra is a wide double star that binoculars split easily.
Mizar and Alcor in the Dipper's handle, a classic naked-eye pair.

southernNote: For southern observers this is early winter: Scorpius climbs high in the east and the Milky Way from the Cross to Sagittarius arches overhead.

title: July: Hercules overhead, the Scorpion below
intro: By the time the July sky is dark, three bright stars dominate the east: [[star:Vega|Vega]], highest and brightest; [[star:Deneb|Deneb]] to its lower left; and [[star:Altair|Altair]] to the lower right. They form the [[asterism:summer-triangle|Summer Triangle]], your signpost until autumn.

From Vega look west to find the [[asterism:keystone|Keystone]] of [[con:Her|Hercules]] nearly overhead, then the half-ring of [[con:CrB|Corona Borealis]], then orange [[star:Arcturus|Arcturus]] in the west. Below Hercules is the big, dim house shape of [[con:Oph|Ophiuchus]], the serpent bearer, holding [[con:Ser|Serpens]].

Now look low in the south. Red [[star:Antares|Antares]] marks the heart of Scorpius, with a row of three stars for the head to its right and the tail curling down to the horizon. Scorpius never rises high from New York, so find a spot with a clear southern view. To its left the Teapot of Sagittarius is rising, and between them is the direction of the center of the Milky Way.

objects.note: The Hercules globular cluster, almost overhead: the best in the northern sky.
A second, smaller globular in Hercules, north of the Keystone.
A loose globular cluster just west of Antares; needs a clear, dark southern sky.
The Ring Nebula between the two bottom stars of Lyra: a tiny smoke ring.
The Double Double near Vega: binoculars show two stars, a telescope at 150× shows each is double again.

southernNote: From the south, Scorpius passes overhead in its full glory and the center of the Milky Way is high in the sky all evening.

title: August: the Summer Triangle and the Milky Way
intro: In August the [[asterism:summer-triangle|Summer Triangle]] is overhead. [[star:Vega|Vega]] is almost at the zenith, [[star:Deneb|Deneb]] is to the east of it and [[star:Altair|Altair]] halfway up the southern sky. Each belongs to its own constellation: the small parallelogram of [[con:Lyr|Lyra]], the long cross of [[con:Cyg|Cygnus]] the swan flying south down the Milky Way, and [[con:Aql|Aquila]] the eagle.

Inside and around the Triangle are three small figures worth learning: the arrow [[con:Sge|Sagitta]], the faint fox [[con:Vul|Vulpecula]] above it, and to the east the neat kite of [[con:Del|Delphinus]] the dolphin. At the foot of the Northern Cross, [[star:Albireo|Albireo]] marks the swan's head.

If you can get to a dark place, this is the month for the Milky Way. It runs from Cassiopeia in the northeast, through Cygnus overhead, down past Aquila and the bright cloud of [[con:Sct|Scutum]] to the Teapot of Sagittarius low in the south, where it is widest and brightest. West of it, [[con:Oph|Ophiuchus]] and [[con:Her|Hercules]] are still high.

objects.note: A showpiece double star: one gold, one blue, split at low power.
The Ring Nebula in Lyra, a planetary nebula, now overhead.
The Dumbbell Nebula near Sagitta, a small gray glow in binoculars from a dark site.
The Wild Duck Cluster in Scutum, a dense open cluster off the tail of Aquila.
The Lagoon Nebula above the Teapot's spout; low in the south, so pick a clear horizon.
A bright globular cluster beside the Teapot's lid.

southernNote: Southern observers see Sagittarius and the galactic center straight overhead, with the Summer Triangle low in the north.

title: September: the Swan flies overhead
intro: September evenings are dark early and still mild. Look straight up for the [[asterism:northern-cross|Northern Cross]]: [[star:Deneb|Deneb]] at the top, [[star:Albireo|Albireo]] at the foot, and a crossbar through [[star:Sadr|Sadr]]. This is [[con:Cyg|Cygnus]], the swan, and the three stars of the Summer Triangle are still high around it.

South of the Cross, [[star:Altair|Altair]] and [[con:Aql|Aquila]] stand high, with the little arrow [[con:Sge|Sagitta]] and the dolphin [[con:Del|Delphinus]] nearby. Farther down in the south is a large, dim triangle like a wide smile: [[con:Cap|Capricornus]], the sea-goat.

The season is turning. In the east the [[asterism:great-square|Great Square of Pegasus]] is up, standing on one corner like a baseball diamond, and in the northeast the W of Cassiopeia is climbing. Between Cassiopeia and Deneb, the house-shaped [[con:Cep|Cepheus]] is at its highest. In the west, Arcturus is setting.

objects.note: Gold and blue double star at the foot of the Northern Cross.
The Dumbbell Nebula, high in the south: the easiest planetary nebula.
The Ring Nebula in Lyra.
The Coathanger, a charming upside-down hanger of ten stars between Albireo and Sagitta.
A compact globular cluster off the nose of Pegasus, beyond the star Enif.
Herschel's Garnet Star, one of the reddest stars visible, below the base of Cepheus.

southernNote: From the south, the Summer Triangle is low in the north while Fomalhaut and the bright star Achernar rise in the southeast.

title: October: the Great Square rises
intro: October's signpost is a big, nearly empty box of four stars high in the southeast: the [[asterism:great-square|Great Square of Pegasus]]. Each side is about a fist and a half long, and none of the four stars is very bright, so let your eyes settle. It is the body of [[con:Peg|Pegasus]], the winged horse, who flies upside down with his neck and head stretching west to the star [[star:Enif|Enif]].

From the Square's top-left corner, [[star:Alpheratz|Alpheratz]], two gently curving chains of stars run northeast: [[con:And|Andromeda]]. Above her, the W of [[con:Cas|Cassiopeia]] is high in the northeast, with [[con:Cep|Cepheus]] and the small zigzag of [[con:Lac|Lacerta]] beside it. The Summer Triangle is still high in the west.

The south is a dim, watery part of the sky: [[con:Aqr|Aquarius]] and [[con:Cap|Capricornus]] have no bright stars. One star stands out all alone, low in the south: [[star:Fomalhaut|Fomalhaut]], sometimes called the lonely star of autumn. Find it by running a line down the right-hand side of the Square and continuing about four and a half fists.

objects.note: The Andromeda Galaxy, 2.5 million light-years away; naked eye from a dark site.
Globular cluster near Enif, the nose of Pegasus.
Globular cluster in Aquarius, a small round glow.
The Double Cluster, rising in the northeast below Cassiopeia.
The original Cepheid variable star: it brightens and fades every 5.4 days.

southernNote: Southern observers see Pegasus low in the north and Fomalhaut nearly overhead, with the Magellanic Clouds high in the south.

title: November: Andromeda and the royal family
intro: On November evenings the [[asterism:great-square|Great Square of Pegasus]] is high in the south, and the constellations of one Greek myth surround it. From the corner star [[star:Alpheratz|Alpheratz]], the chained princess [[con:And|Andromeda]] stretches northeast, almost overhead. Her mother, [[con:Cas|Cassiopeia]], is the W high in the north; her father, [[con:Cep|Cepheus]], is beside it; and her rescuer [[con:Per|Perseus]] follows in the northeast.

Below Andromeda are three small figures: the thin triangle of [[con:Tri|Triangulum]], the short bent line of [[con:Ari|Aries]] with its bright star [[star:Hamal|Hamal]], and under the Square a faint ring of stars, the Circlet of [[con:Psc|Pisces]]. South and east of them sprawls the sea monster [[con:Cet|Cetus]], large and dim.

In the east, winter is announcing itself: the Pleiades are well up, followed by orange [[star:Aldebaran|Aldebaran]] and bright [[star:Capella|Capella]]. In the west, the Summer Triangle is sinking, with the Northern Cross soon to stand upright on the horizon.

objects.note: The Andromeda Galaxy, now passing nearly overhead: the farthest thing you can see without a telescope.
The Triangulum Galaxy, large and very faint; only from a truly dark site.
The Double Cluster between Cassiopeia and Perseus.
A fine gold and blue double star at the end of Andromeda's chain.
The Demon Star: every 2.87 days it dims noticeably for a few hours as a fainter companion eclipses it.
The Pleiades, climbing in the east.

southernNote: From the south, the Great Square is low in the north, Achernar is high, and both Magellanic Clouds are well placed.

title: December: Perseus overhead, winter rising
intro: Long December nights start with the [[asterism:cassiopeia-w|W of Cassiopeia]] high in the north, tipped over into an M. From it, follow the Milky Way toward the east and you come to [[con:Per|Perseus]], almost overhead: a curved line of stars around its brightest, [[star:Mirfak|Mirfak]], with the famous variable star [[star:Algol|Algol]] to the south.

Continue down the same line and you reach brilliant [[star:Capella|Capella]] in [[con:Aur|Auriga]], then the Pleiades and the V of [[con:Tau|Taurus]] with orange [[star:Aldebaran|Aldebaran]], all high in the east. Below them Orion is clearing the horizon, lying on his side with the Belt pointing straight up.

To the west of the zenith, [[con:And|Andromeda]], [[con:Tri|Triangulum]] and [[con:Ari|Aries]] are high, and the Great Square of Pegasus is tilting down toward the west. The dim sea monster [[con:Cet|Cetus]] fills the south.

objects.note: The Pleiades, high in the east; count the stars by eye, then try binoculars.
The Hyades, the V of Taurus, beside Aldebaran.
The Double Cluster, nearly overhead between Perseus and Cassiopeia.
An open cluster in Perseus, between Algol and Almach; a small hazy patch in binoculars.
The Andromeda Galaxy, still high in the west.
A red giant in Cetus that swings from naked-eye visibility to invisibility over about eleven months.

southernNote: Southern observers enjoy summer nights with Orion rising in the east, Achernar and Canopus high, and the Magellanic Clouds at their best.
